steps.body: Every measurement has a limit to how finely it was taken. Combine two measurements — add them, subtract them, divide one by the other — and the result can be no MORE precise than the least precise input. A slope computed from whole-centimetre data cannot honestly claim five decimal places, however many the calculator displays.
Plant height (nearest cm) over 5 days. Fit the growth rate.

predict.prompt: A plant's height was measured to the nearest whole centimetre on five different days, then a growth rate was fitted. Should the reported slope have more decimal places than the height data, the same, or fewer?

options.label: About the same — matching the data's own precision
More — decimals make it look more scientific

predict.reveal: About the same. A calculated slope inherits its honest precision from the data that produced it — reporting more decimals than the input supports is precision the data never actually promised.

widget.prompt: Fit a line to day (x) versus height in cm (y), each measured to the nearest whole cm.
widget.successFeedback: About 2.5 cm/day. That single extra decimal place is reasonable — one more digit than the whole-centimetre readings, not five.
widget.slopeFeedback: Adjust the tilt to follow this rising trend.
widget.offsetFeedback: The tilt is close; slide toward the cloud's centre.

steps.body: Judge whether a reported precision is appropriate.
explanationVariants: The height data only supports whole centimetres, so a rate stretched to five decimals claims certainty the measurements never had.
More decimal places is not automatically more correct — it can just be false precision.

widget.prompt: The fitted rate comes out to 2.5 cm/day. A report writes it as '2.50000 cm/day'. Is that appropriate?

options.label: No — the data was only measured to the nearest cm, so five decimals is false precision
options.feedback: The height readings themselves were whole numbers. A rate built from them can be trusted to about one extra decimal, not five — the calculator's extra digits are noise, not information.

options.label: Yes — more decimal places always means a more accurate answer
options.feedback: The digits have to be EARNED by the data's own precision. A calculator will happily print digits the measurements never supported.

options.label: No — it should be rounded to the nearest whole number instead
options.feedback: Whole-cm inputs support roughly one extra decimal in a computed rate, which is more than zero decimals but far short of five.

options.label: It doesn't matter as long as the number is correct
options.feedback: A number can be arithmetically correct and still overstate its own precision — that overstatement is the actual problem here.

steps.body: Apply the rule to a concrete sum.
explanationVariants: 6 cm + 3.4 cm = 9.4 cm, but the whole-cm measurement caps the honest precision at the nearest whole cm: 9.
Add normally, then round to the LESS precise measurement's precision, not the more precise one.

widget.prompt: A rectangle's sides are 6 cm (nearest cm) and 3.4 cm (nearest mm). Add them, then round to the LESS precise measurement's precision. What's the sum?

commonErrors.feedback: 9.4 keeps the millimetre measurement's extra digit, which the whole-cm side can't back up. Round to the nearest whole cm: 9.
3 only uses one of the two measurements. Add both, then round: 6 + 3.4 = 9.4, rounds to 9.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 6 + 3.4 = 9.4, rounded to the coarser whole-cm precision: 9.

steps.body: The rule in one line: **a result is only as precise as its least precise input.** Add, subtract, multiply, or divide measurements together, and whichever one was measured most coarsely sets the ceiling for how many meaningful digits the answer can honestly claim — no arithmetic operation manufactures precision that wasn't in the data to begin with.
A 240 mg sample (measured to the nearest 10 mg) loses mass over 5 measured intervals. Build the decay trend.

widget.prompt: Two reported masses, 240 mg and 90 mg, both rounded to the nearest 10 mg. Their gap is 150 mg. Report the gap to a sensible precision: how many 10 mg units is it?

measureChoices.feedback: 150 mg is the raw gap, correct as a value but stated to single-mg precision the 10 mg-rounded inputs don't support. In units of the 10 mg precision, that's 15.
150 mg of gap, measured in units of the shared 10 mg precision, is 15 of those units — matching what both inputs can honestly support.
240 is one of the original masses, not the gap between them.

widget.successFeedback: 15 units of 10 mg each — 150 mg, reported no finer than the measurements that produced it. The gap can't be more precise than the numbers that made it.

steps.body: Apply the least-precise-wins rule to a new pair.
explanationVariants: 18 cm (nearest cm) and 7.2 cm (nearest mm): the difference can only be trusted to the nearest cm, since that is the coarser input.
Find the coarsest input's precision, then hold the answer to that.

widget.prompt: A wall is 18 cm long (nearest cm) and a shelf is 7.2 cm (nearest mm). Report their difference to the LESS precise measurement's precision — the nearest whole cm.

commonErrors.feedback: 10.8 keeps the shelf's finer millimetre precision, which the whole-cm wall measurement can't back up. Round to the nearest cm: 11.
25.2 adds the lengths instead of subtracting them.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 18 − 7.2 = 10.8, rounded to the coarser cm precision: 11.

steps.body: Spot false precision in the wild.
explanationVariants: A odometer reading to the nearest tenth of a mile cannot support a claimed 8-decimal average speed — the input's coarseness caps the output's.
However many digits a calculator shows, the input measurement's precision is still the ceiling.
hints: Look at how precisely the DISTANCE was actually measured.
Tenths of a mile is roughly one extra decimal of trustworthy precision in a computed rate, not eight.
The display showing more digits doesn't mean those digits are meaningful.

widget.prompt: A car's trip odometer reads distance to the nearest 0.1 mile. A phone app computes average speed as '47.28193651 mph'. What's wrong?

options.label: The distance was only measured to one decimal place, so the speed shouldn't claim eight
options.feedback: The 0.1-mile odometer is the precision ceiling. A computed rate can reasonably carry one extra digit of confidence, not eight — the phone is just displaying every digit its calculator produced, meaningful or not.

options.label: Nothing is wrong — more decimals means a more exact answer
options.feedback: The extra decimals are computational noise, not real information, once the input's own coarseness is accounted for.

options.label: The speed should be a whole number with no decimals at all
options.feedback: Some extra precision beyond the input is reasonable in a computed rate — the problem is EIGHT decimals, not any decimals.

options.label: The odometer must be broken if the app shows that many digits
options.feedback: The odometer is fine — the app is simply reporting more digits than the input can honestly support.

steps.body: A result can't be more precise than its least precise ingredient.
takeaways: Combining measurements — adding, subtracting, computing a rate — never manufactures precision beyond the coarsest input.
A calculator's extra displayed digits are not automatically meaningful; they can be pure noise past what the data supports.
Match a reported result's precision to the LEAST precise measurement that built it, not the most precise.
steps.teaser: That closes this course: describing data, fitting and grading a model, and reporting it honestly.

concept.body: Rewind. If one measurement is precise to the nearest whole unit and another to the nearest tenth, a result built from BOTH can only be trusted to the COARSER of the two — the whole unit, not the tenth.

explanationVariants: The coarser measurement (nearest whole cm) sets the limit, so 5 cm is the honest precision.
Match the LEAST precise input, always.

widget.prompt: One length is measured to the nearest cm (5 cm); another to the nearest mm (3.2 cm). Their sum should be reported to the nearest:

options.label: Whole cm — matching the coarser measurement
options.feedback: The 5 cm reading is the weaker link; the sum can't be trusted beyond what THAT measurement supports.

options.label: Millimetre — matching the finer measurement
options.feedback: The finer measurement doesn't rescue the coarser one; the coarser one still caps the result.
